Why these rows look so flat
The strongest average share anywhere in this table is only

for a perfectly even row, because this model has not been trained: an untrained decoder spreads its attention fairly evenly over every source word it is allowed to see. Training is what turns these rows into sharp peaks, typically on the source word that
matches what is being written. The shape, the masking and the axes are already exactly what the final heatmap shows — only the sharpness changes.
C · The three attention blocks, side by side
the same class, three sets of arguments
Three attention blocks, one class, three sets of arguments
Cross-attention is easiest to understand by comparison. Everything that makes it special is in this table, and none of it is in the class.
square · every word sees the whole sentence
RECTANGULAR · no causal mask — the whole source is fair game
self-attention → cross-attention → feed-forward, each reading a normalised copy
The decoder layer as a whole, in the order it runs

had two sub-layers; the decoder has three, and the extra one is the only place the two halves of the model touch. The order is not arbitrary — read the middle column from top to bottom as a sentence and the design explains itself.

Why cross-attention sits in the middle
Each layer reads the source exactly once, in the middle. Sub-
works out what has been written so far; sub-
fetches whatever the source says about
processes the result, one position at a time. Put cross-attention first and the decoder would be asking the source for help before it had looked at
its own output — it would have nothing specific to ask about. With

This is pre-norm — the newer of the two arrangements
works on a COPY, before the sub-layer, and the main path is only ever added to. That is
pre-norm. It trains more stably than the original arrangement, which is why deep models use it —
adds a learning-rate warm-up anyway, for safety. The cost
is that the stack no longer ends at a predictable scale, which is why
the difference is hard to see; at
